en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-bodhisattvādhyātma-śīla-sūtra*,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of North India during the Song Dynasty.
On the fifteenth day, when the Buddha was reciting the precepts, Mañjuśrī adjusted his robes and, with his head...
Placing his head at the Buddha’s feet, he rose to kneel and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If there is a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment, what merits should they employ—whether in the path of the world or the secular realm—to transform and enlighten all sentient beings, so that each may achieve their own merit?”
"Only the Buddha should, through his skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), analyze and explain this for us!
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
Mañjuśrī! What you have asked is most profound, most profound; it brings great transcendence and provides great peace.
If you listen attentively and receive it with care, I shall explain its essentials for you in detail; each of you should then put them into practice according to your own understanding.
All those present in the assembly and Mañjuśrī replied,
"We shall receive your instructions. The Buddha said:
"First, one should take the triple refuge in the Three Honored Ones, saying:

'I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the Bhikṣu Saṃgha; I take refuge in the Bodhisattvas; I take refuge in the Mahāsattvas; I take refuge in Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; I take refuge in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.'"
I have committed evil with my body, spoken evil with my mouth, and harbored evil thoughts in my mind; not knowing that I was doing so intentionally, I shall not do so again.

For a hundred thousand kalpas, the Bodhisattva path has constantly practiced the four immeasurable minds; since those hundred thousand kalpas, I have committed evil with my body, spoken evil with my mouth, and harbored evil thoughts in my mind; not knowing that I was doing so intentionally, I shall not do so again.
"In my previous lives, I did not practice the bodhisattva path; now, I am practicing this bodhisattva path.
Because I have abandoned evil, from this day forward I shall perform good deeds day and night, and dare not again commit any evils."
“Pāraṇajyotipāla, a bodhisattva who has first resolved [to attain enlightenment] should practice the six pāramitās.
What are the six?
First is dānapāramitā (the perfection of giving):”
The mental activity of generosity;
second, the mental activity of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*); and the mental activity of... [the third].
The third is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*):
the mental practice of forbearance;
the fourth is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*):
The mental activity of diligence;
the fifth, the perfection of dhyāna:
the mental activity of one-pointed concentration.
The sixth is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā):
the mental activity of wisdom.
If one sees others distributing gifts in charity, one should cultivate a sincere mind and rejoice on their behalf.
If one sees someone upholding the precepts, one should with a sincere mind rejoice on their behalf;
if one sees someone practicing patience, one should with a sincere mind rejoice on their behalf;
if one sees someone practicing diligence, one should with a sincere mind rejoice on their behalf.
If one sees someone sitting in meditation, one should with a sincere mind rejoice on their behalf;
if one sees someone preaching the sutras with wisdom, one should with a sincere mind rejoice on their behalf.
A bodhisattva should know that these three vows constitute being a bodhisattva.
What are the three? First, the vow:

"May I become a Buddha; when I become a Buddha, may there be no three evil realms in my land, and may it abound in the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli. May the lifespan of the people be infinite, and may they all naturally obtain food, clothing, the five kinds of music, performers, and palaces.
Second, the vow: "May I be reborn before Amitābha Buddha."
Third, may I encounter the Buddha in every lifetime, and may the Buddha grant me a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
These are the three vows; taken together with the others, they constitute the fifteen precepts, which a bodhisattva should fully practice and uphold.

Vaira is named "The Enlightened Teacher," and Aṅgīra is named "Mañjuśrī. All bodhisattvas of the past who preceded us first conceived the aspiration for enlightenment and practiced the bodhisattva path at Pālañjidūpa, thereby attaining Buddhahood for themselves.
Yet, there is neither a bodhisattva path nor a Buddha; for this reason, one should practice the bodhisattva path and become a Buddha.
"There are five matters concerning a bodhisattva entering Song Temple:
when entering Song Temple, one must not wear straw sandals;
one must not carry a parasol or canopy when entering Song Temple."
One should pay homage to the Buddha, circumambulate the stupa three times, and enter Song Temple;
if one sees impurity or filth, one should sweep it away before entering Song Temple;
upon seeing any śramaṇas, one should perform prostrations to them all.
"There are two matters regarding the path traveled by a bodhisattva:
when it is hot or during rain, upon seeing trees or dwellings, one should yield the place to others first to sit;
if one sees well-water, spring water, or someone carrying water, one should yield it for them to drink; only if one sees a great river or stream may one drink oneself."
These are the two matters.
"When a bodhisattva receives food or drink from others, there are three matters:
they observe both those above and below them and ensure that all are treated equally."
If the portions are not equal, one should divide them so that they are equal.

After the meal, when receiving water to drink, one should yield the right to the senior monk (upādhyāya) to drink first. Once he has drunk, one must not rise and depart before him; rather, one should rise together with the assembly.
"These are the ten rules of conduct.
At the first assembly: "Homage to the Buddha!
Now I receive the forty-seven precepts of the *śīla*."
What are the forty-seven?

First, a bodhisattva must not kill living beings; they must not engage in killing through body, speech, or mind, nor entertain thoughts of killing. One who entertains thoughts of killing cannot be a bodhisattva.
"Second, a bodhisattva must not steal the property of others.
Third, a bodhisattva must not commit adultery with the wives or daughters of others.
Fourth, a bodhisattva must not deceive or neglect others."
"Fifth, a bodhisattva must not drink alcohol.
Sixth, a bodhisattva must not engage in double-tongued speech.
Seventh, a bodhisattva must not engage in harsh speech."
"Eighth, a bodhisattva must not speak falsely.
Ninth, a bodhisattva must not engage in frivolous speech.
Tenth, a bodhisattva must not harbor jealousy."
"Eleventh, a bodhisattva must not harbor anger.
Twelfth, a bodhisattva must not harbor delusion or doubt.
Thirteenth, a bodhisattva must not place faith in the paths of demonic heretics."
"Fourteenth, a bodhisattva must not teach others to engage in unwholesome conduct.
Fifteenth, a bodhisattva should extensively employ skillful means to benefit others through giving."
"Sixteenth, a bodhisattva must not be stingy or greedy.
Seventeenth, a bodhisattva must not covet the wealth and property of others.
Eighteenth, a bodhisattva must not harm others with a malicious mind."
"Nineteenth, a bodhisattva must not slander or strike others.
Twentieth, a bodhisattva must not whip or beat others.
Twenty-first, a bodhisattva must not plunder free citizens to make them slaves."
"Twenty-second, a bodhisattva must not engage in the trade of slaves.
Twenty-third, a bodhisattva must not sell his wife or children to others."
"Twenty-fourth: A bodhisattva must not engage in mutual sexual dalliance with men or women.
Twenty-fifth: A bodhisattva must not go to gambling dens or the houses of prostitutes."
"Twenty-sixth, a bodhisattva must not go to the home of a eunuch.
Twenty-seventh, a bodhisattva must not engage in mutual deception or fraud.
Twenty-eighth, a bodhisattva must not use heavy weights to exploit others."
"Twenty-ninth, a bodhisattva must not deceive others by using light weights.
Thirtieth, a bodhisattva must not encroach upon others by using large measuring cups."
"Thirty-first, a bodhisattva must not deceive others by using a small measuring cup.
Thirty-second, a bodhisattva must not encroach upon others by using an overly long measuring rod."
"Thirty-third: A bodhisattva must not deceive others by using a short measuring rod.
Thirty-fourth: A bodhisattva must not deprive oxen or horses of their five aggregates."
"Thirty-fifth, a bodhisattva must not sell oxen or horses.
Thirty-sixth, a bodhisattva must not sell elephants or camels.
Thirty-seventh, a bodhisattva must not sell mules or donkeys."
"Thirty-eighth, a bodhisattva must not sell pigs or sheep.
Thirty-ninth, a bodhisattva must not sell chickens, dogs, or other livestock."
"Fortieth: A bodhisattva must not sell the Dharma of the sutras.
Forty-first: A bodhisattva must not go to the homes of those who follow demonic paths.
Forty-second: A bodhisattva must not go to the homes of those of the caste that carries out the dead."
“Forty-third, a bodhisattva must not enter a household where there is mourning for the dead.
Forty-fourth, a bodhisattva must not enter a tavern.
Forty-fifth, a bodhisattva must not enter a soup-and-rice shop.”
“Forty-sixth: When a bodhisattva receives food from others, he thinks to himself:
‘When shall I practice giving to others so that they may be fully satisfied, just as I am today?’”

"Forty-seventh: When Bodhisattvas see one another, their hearts should be filled with joy, just as they would upon seeing their own parents or brothers; they should regard others in this same way, without any distinction."
If you see someone practicing the path of a bodhisattva, you should regard them with an impartial mind and must not say that one person is good while another is evil.
This constitutes the forty-seventh precept for being fully endowed as a bodhisattva.
One must not commit the ten evil deeds through body, speech, or mind; one must not teach others to commit them, nor should one encourage others to do so.
Day and night, one should reflect:
"I uphold these precepts, remaining firm and unshakable; I shall surely attain the three skills."
First, they shall attain the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika);
second, they shall attain the stage of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
third, they shall become Buddhas.
"In the second period: 'Homage to the Buddha!
Now I shall receive the four gates of the *kṣānti-avaivartika* dharma.
What are the four?'"
The twenty causal conditions of the Buddha, the twenty causal conditions of the Dharma, the twenty causal conditions of the body, and the twenty causal conditions of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
"What are the twenty causal conditions of a Buddha?

These are the practices of a Buddha, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha: the initial resolve of the mind; the divine eye that perceives clearly and foreknows what others are thinking in their hearts;

the three types of *śukla-dharma* (pure conduct) practiced through body, speech, and mind; these three types of *śukla-dharma* are the removal of the three hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), which leads to the formation of *sugati* (a happy rebirth); and *sugati* is *nirvāṇa*."
Kāpita, the Father of the World;
Anuttara, him above whom there is none in the heavens or on earth; Puluosha, the valiant man.
Dharmasārathi: "Dharma" means the Dharma; "Sārathi" means one who governs the world through the Dharma.
Devamanuṣyaśāstā: the Buddha who teaches gods and men in heaven and on earth. Bhūmipratiṣṭhitapāda:
his feet tread upon the ground with soles that are level.
When walking, he lifts his feet straight;
the spaces between his fingers and toes are joined by webs of skin;
and his complexion is the color of purple-polished gold.
His two hands, two shoulders, and neck have soft flesh;
his jaw is like that of a lion;
he has forty teeth that are perfectly white and even.
The tongue extends beyond the mouth; it enters the ears, the eyes, and the nose, and covers the face of its own accord;
there is the fleshly protuberance on the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*). These are the twenty causes and conditions of a Buddha.
"What are the twenty causal conditions of the Dharma?
They are: *āśuṣa* as fundamental ignorance;
that which is done by *saṃkāra*;..."
Veyyāraṇa knows all matters; Nāmaluva:
*nāma* means name, and *luva* means what is seen by the eye;
Sālayatana: merit and demerit, the phenomena that arrive.
Pāli: Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; feeling (*vedanā*), contact (*phassa*), and craving (*taṇhā*);
when a disease has not yet been cured, there is the pain of distress, and when a disease has already been cured, there is the pleasant pain—these are the three roots:
*nāgamaddana*, *pavusaddana*, and *vipasaddana*.
That which is beloved by men and women;
the wish to become a deva or a human; the wish that my own body be wealthy and noble without limit;
the *upādhyāya* who causes his disciple to receive instruction and perform the *praṇidhāna*; and the accomplishment of that deed, which brings about birth among the people of the world.
Jāramaraṇa (old age and death), jāra (old age), and maraṇa (death).
These constitute the twelve links of dependent origination of birth and death.
There are four intentions.
What are the four?

They are the application of mindfulness to the body, the application of mindfulness to feelings, the application of mindfulness to the mind, and the application of mindfulness to phenomena; these are called the four applications of mindfulness.
The four bases of psychic power are desire, energy, mind, and wisdom; these are the four bases of psychic power.
These are the twenty kinds of causal conditions for dharmas.
What are the twenty causal conditions for the body?
They are the three matters performed by the body.
What are the three?
Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
One must not kill oneself, nor should one instruct others to kill;
One must not steal oneself, nor should one instruct others to steal;
one must not engage in sexual misconduct oneself, nor should one instruct others to engage in sexual misconduct.
These four matters pertain to what is done by way of speech.
What are the four?
Divisive speech, harsh speech, false speech, and frivolous speech.
One should not engage in divisive speech oneself, nor should one instruct others to engage in divisive speech.
Not speaking harsh words oneself, one must not teach others to speak harsh words;
not speaking falsely oneself, one must not teach others to speak falsely;
not speaking frivolously oneself, one must not teach others to speak frivolously.
Three matters are produced by the mind.
What are the three?
Envy, ill-will, and delusive doubt.
If one’s own mind is not envious, one must not teach others to be envious;
if one’s own mind is not angry, one must not teach others to be angry;
if one’s own mind is not deluded or doubtful, one must not teach others to be deluded or doubtful.
One must not transgress these ten matters through body, speech, or mind, nor should one teach others to transgress them.
These constitute the twenty types of causal conditions for the dharmas of body, speech, and mind.
"What are the twenty causal conditions of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā? They are:

the aspiration formed in previous lives to cause all people in the world to become Buddhas; the aspiration to cause all people in the world to possess the power of clairvoyance; and the aspiration to cause all people in the world to possess the power of clairaudience."
Pārāśarya knew the thoughts of people’s minds, desiring that all people in the world know the thoughts of people’s minds.
Aṅgiras, Aṅgiras, and Raibhya knew the thoughts in the minds of all people in the world, desiring that all people in the world know the thoughts in the minds of all people.
Ānanda, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are dependent; this is known by the Buddha, whom he desires all people in the world to know.
The Buddha manifested his majestic spiritual power, desiring that all people throughout the world know it.
Mahākātyāyana, the Buddha, with a heart of compassion, thought of all people throughout the world, desiring that all people throughout the world [attain understanding].
The *Sāmbhūtarāṇa* knows all human affairs throughout the world and desires that all people in the world likewise know all such affairs.

The *Anāśvarāṇa* possesses a Buddha-wisdom that none of the ghosts, spirits, celestial deities, or dragon deities throughout the world can restrain; he desires that all people in the world know this wisdom.
These are the twenty kinds of causal conditions for the Mahāprajñāpāramitā; when combined, they constitute the eighty kinds of causal conditions for the dharma of the avaivartika bodhisattva.
Because past, future, and present bodhisattvas all assemble through these eighty kinds of causes and conditions, this constitutes the dharma of a bodhisattva.
The third period: "Homage to the Buddha!
Now, by receiving the twenty causal conditions for the Dharma of *vīrya* (diligence), one knows one's own past lives through the practice thereof.
What are these twenty?..."
There are five causes and conditions for great merit.

What are the five? Great merit from the gift of giving (*dāna*); great merit from the precepts (*śīla*); great merit from mindfulness (*smṛti*); immeasurable merit from the wholesome deeds one performs; and immeasurable merit from governing and maintaining a monastery.
These five bring much merit.
There are five causes and conditions for protecting the body.
What are these five protections?
Protection of the body, protection of speech, protection of the mind, protection through the precepts (*śīla*), and protection through the vows (*vinaya*).
These are the five causes and conditions for protecting the body.
"The Bodhisattva has five intentions."
What are the five?

They are the intention of moral discipline, the intention of a benevolent mind, the intention of a kind heart, the intention of generosity, and the intention of mindfulness toward the path of goodness and wisdom.
These are the five intentions.
Combining these, there are twenty kinds of causal conditions; by practicing them and knowing one's own past lives, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What is meant by "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*)?
"In the heavens above and on the earth below, there is none who stands above him.
During the fourth period, he said: "Namo Buddha!
Now I receive the Dharma of the four dhyānas."
What is the method of dhyāna?
When a bodhisattva sits in meditation with a single-minded focus on recollecting the Buddha, the mind comes to rest upon the fact that the Buddha is empty and non-existent.
Furthermore, by reflecting on the five desires of greed and lust, and realizing that these five desires of greed and lust do not exist, one attains the first dhyāna.

When a bodhisattva sits in meditation with a single-minded focus on the Dharma, that Dharma is also empty and non-existent; thus, the mind is free from anger and the sensations of pain or pleasure. Being free from anger and the sensations of pain or pleasure, he thus attains the second dhyāna.

When a bodhisattva sits in meditation with a single-minded focus on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, it is also empty and non-existent; thus, the mind is free from delusion, and he thus attains the third dhyāna.
Having attained the third dhyāna, all evils are exhausted and there is nothing further to be thought of; the mind is pure, unmoving, and unshakable, and he thus attains the fourth dhyāna.
"With a single mind that no longer wavers, one naturally attains the five supernormal powers; this is the Bodhisattva’s practice of the dharma of meditation.
At the fifth stage: "Namo Buddha!
Now I receive the dharma of the Prajñā-samādhi."
What is called the Dharma of Samādhi?

The samādhi of a bodhisattva consists of compassionately regarding all those in the ten directions—gods, humans, parents, brothers, wives, children, enemies, creditors, those in the hells (niraya), hungry ghosts (preta), animals, and all others in distress and hardship, whether human or non-human, including *sahṛtsa*—wishing for them all to be liberated from suffering and to attain rebirth in the human realm, where they may practice the six *pāramitās* and the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is the Dharma of the bodhisattva’s samādhi.

"The Bodhisattva’s samādhi consists of maintaining an impartial mind toward all those in the ten directions—gods, humans, parents, brothers, wives, children, enemies, creditors, those in the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans and non-humans, and even those who are not *sakhya*—desiring to bring them all liberation from their hardships, providing them with wealth, joy, peace, and security, and causing them to resolve upon the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is the dharma of the Bodhisattva’s samādhi."

“The Bodhisattva’s samādhi consists of an impartial mind and a heart of loving-kindness, feeling compassion for all those in the ten directions—gods, humans, parents, brothers, wives, children, enemies, creditors, beings in the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans and non-humans, and *sahṛdayas*—regarding and protecting them just as a mother regards and protects her infant. Being equal toward all without any discriminatory thought; this equality is the dharma of samādhi.”
From this, one naturally attains the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Whether sitting or rising, the Bodhisattva should contemplate day and night, always maintaining an even mind and equanimous intent; this is the dharma of the Bodhisattva’s samādhi.
At the sixth stage: "Homage to the Buddhas! Homage to the Bodhisattvas! Homage to the Mahāsattvas!
Now I receive the dharma of samādhi, just as the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas do."

Now I maintain my mind so that all I do shall be like empty space; now I maintain emptiness to create equanimity. Therefore, in practicing the bodhisattva path, I maintain my mind to view the myriad people of the world as one, regarding them just as I would my own parents, brothers, wife, and children, without distinction, and viewing them with an impartial heart.
"Now I rejoice in performing good deeds for the people of the worlds throughout the ten directions; this is the samādhi of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
To those who maintain the precepts of this samādhi, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī shall come to converse with them, saying:
'Those who maintain the precepts of this samādhi are the most honored among all bodhisattvas.'"
"This is the Samādhi of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī.
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī-Samādhi is about to rise from his seat, he joins his palms and reflects upon the vow within his heart, saying:
'I am a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva; it is through the practice of giving and distribution performed by me as Mañjuśrī-Bodhisattva that I have attained the path of a Bodhisattva.'"
If someone asks a bodhisattva for his eyes, the bodhisattva should give him his eyes;
if someone asks for his body, the bodhisattva should give him his body;
if someone asks for wealth and goods, the bodhisattva should give him that wealth and goods!
One should constantly reflect, saying:
"I am a bodhisattva, and Mañjuśrī is also a bodhisattva; now I shall truly maintain this body with non-falsity."

A bodhisattva should constantly keep in mind that the people of the world throughout the ten directions be secure, peaceful, wealthy, and happy; should they be subject to toil and suffering, the bodhisattva should resolve to bring them security, peace, wealth, happiness, and liberation.

A bodhisattva should earnestly maintain the dharmas of the body and practice the bodhisattva path; a bodhisattva should urgently desire to become a śramaṇa and uphold the dhyāna-pāramitā, thinking: "I must quickly go to the presence of Amitābha Buddha; upholding this samādhi, I urgently desire to meet and enjoy myself with those made of crystal, lapis lazuli, gold, and silver."
“Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, *vatsa* is named *atipara*, and *agha* is named *atitā*. At the seventh period:
“Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Dharma! Homage to the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus! Homage to all Mahāsattvas! Homage to the Bodhisattva Ananyagāmin!”
Abiding in the path of samādhi, he reflects:

"When shall I become a great light like the sun and moon for those among the people of the ten directions who dwell in darkness? When shall I act as a light for the people of the ten directions, just as a bodhisattva should act as a great light for the people of the ten directions?"

"One should truly uphold the mind in this samādhi; one should govern with urgency, settling and balancing the mind, acting as a source of illumination for the people of the ten directions and the world, like the sun and the moon."
This is the path of samādhi for the bodhisattva; it shall serve to level the minds of all people throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Now, there are bodhisattvas in the ten directions who practice samādhi; they employ this "Moon Samādhi. Just as other bodhisattvas employ this samādhi, so too did the Bodhisattva Huṇa-jū-liu ask Śākyamuni Buddha: "What is this samādhi?"
Śākyamuni Buddha remained silent and said nothing.
Puṇyamitra asked again about samādhi, but Śākyamuni Buddha still said nothing.
Bodhisattva Puṇyamitra thought to himself:
"What is the Buddha’s state of mind?

When Haṇa-guliu perceived the Buddha’s mind, he rose and went to pay homage to the Buddha. Haṇa-guliu then struck the *gandī* bell; Bodhisattvas from the ten directions who were in samādhi all came to the assembly. After sixty thousand Bodhisattvas had all come forward to pay homage to the Buddha, they all sat down.
Hunajiu asked the Buddha:
"What is the name of the samādhi for impartially benefiting the people of the ten directions and the world, and what is the name of the Moon Samādhi?"

The Buddha said: "Sixty thousand bodhisattvas have all attained equanimity; yet the *kūṭāgāras* all shook and could not remain stable. The Buddha’s majestic spiritual power brings peace to the world. This samādhi is named the Moon Samādhi (*candraprabha-samādhi*). Those who have heard of this samādhi should all practice it with an equanimous mind."
The Eighth Period: "Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Dharma! Homage to the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus! Homage to all Bodhisattvas! Homage to the Mahāsattvas! Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!"

I reflect that in my previous lives I have already practiced the bodhisattva path; I reflect that I have served three hundred billion Buddhas; and I reflect that when I was a bodhisattva in former lives, I constantly used a heart of compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and protection to take pity on all humans, non-humans, and even the crawling and wriggling creatures, always feeling profound sorrow for them. I constantly encouraged and guided them through the Way of the sutras, enabling them to enter the True Dharma, to distance themselves from evil, and to practice goodness.

My ears do not receive sounds of good or evil; my eyes do not look upon forms that are beautiful or ugly; my nose does not smell odors that are fragrant or foul; my mouth does not taste flavors that are savory or bland; my body does not seek adornments that are coarse or fine; my mind does not seek desires that are desirable—I myself have severed these six.
"I have personally severed the three [senses], so that six matters do not arise:
the ear attains concentration and does not hear sounds of good or evil;
the eye attains concentration and does not behold forms of beauty or ugliness."
The nose attains concentration and does not smell odors, whether foul or fragrant;
the mouth attains concentration and does not crave or cling to the five flavors;
the body attains concentration and no longer perceives the sensations of cold, heat, pain, or itching.
The mind attains concentration, free from further thoughts of coming and going.
The body practices the dāna-pāramitā, desiring only to give;
the eyes constitute the śīla-pāramitā, desiring only to maintain the precepts.
The ear is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), desiring only forbearance;
the nose is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), desiring only diligence;
the mouth is the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), desiring only single-mindedness.
My intention is the *prajñāpāramitā*, desiring only wisdom.

I have always used these six matters to rescue and bestow benefits upon all beings; now that I have been born here again, I am able to see the Buddha’s sutras and precepts, and I am further able to serve the Triple Gem.

I shall now further employ six matters to transform and guide all beings, extensively benefiting them through this Dharma-gate, leading the multitude to realize the Great Way, and acting as a guiding leader for all humans and non-humans.
"When death is near, I shall not violate the pure precepts;
when death is near, I shall not be deluded by desire at the time of death;

when death is near, I shall not be moved by what is acceptable or unacceptable—this is my sincere vow. If someone comes to seek my body, I shall give it to them; I will restrain myself from seeking anything else and shall not oppose them. This is what constitutes a bodhisattva."
To maintain the precepts of the nine periods with a mind of equanimity is what constitutes upholding the precepts.

Why is this so? It is for the sake of the Buddhas of the ten directions; it is for the sake of all the sutras and dharmas; it is for the sake of the community of bhikṣus; it is for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; and it is for the sake of all humans and non-humans, as well as the crawling and wriggling creatures throughout the world in the ten directions. Because I uphold these matters and take compassionate concern for sentient beings, I have now attained the path of a bodhisattva and practice the various dharmas of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, the path of the Bodhisattva is difficult to encounter and difficult to hear; those who hear it shall all attain the stage of Avaivartika.
Now, I offer my own body and life to the Buddhas of the ten directions, and with single-minded resolve, I shall never again regress.
The Ninth Period: “Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Dharma! Homage to the Sangha of Bhikṣus! Homage to all Bodhisattvas! Homage to the Mahāsattvas! Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!”
The path of the bodhisattva is extremely difficult; I shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings with my own body and life, without any sense of attachment or regret.

The bodhisattva commits no transgressions, nor does he fear them. When the retribution of past lives arrives and when enemies or creditors come, the bodhisattva faces these with joy to exhaust his debts, remaining neither terrified nor anxious.
The bodhisattva upholds the Dharma according to the Dharma and upholds the precepts according to the precepts; by means of faith, the bodhisattva attains Buddhahood.
The bodhisattva reads widely through the various sutras, enters fully into all paths, and transforms sentient beings in accordance with their needs.
The Bodhisattva constantly practices a mind of loving-kindness; his speech is refined and gentle, never harming the feelings of others.
Even when living together with his wife and children, he treats them as if they were an enemy, always guarding their minds.
A bodhisattva regards women as tigers, wolves, and lions, or as venomous serpents; yet the bodhisattva does not fear them.
Lust cannot move the mind of the bodhisattva. Because the bodhisattva has abandoned desire, lust cannot defile the bodhisattva’s pure conduct.
Just as a lotus does not grow on high mountains or dry land, yet a bodhisattva is born amidst desire and attachment; just as a lotus, though born from within the mud, is not defiled by the mire.

Within the Bodhisattva precepts, inner discipline is not separate from outer conduct. Outer conduct is like the earth, while inner discipline is like water. Water takes purity, gentleness, and softness as its function; the earth takes vast capacity and great receptivity as its merit.
All grasses and trees grow from the earth, and all myriad things live by means of water; therefore, the merit of a bodhisattva is like the earth and like water.
When a bodhisattva dwells alone in the mountains, they are likewise free from fear.
Although a bodhisattva may live at home, supporting a wife and children, they always remain as if dwelling alone; tranquil and stable, they are free from any further thoughts of pain or pleasure.

For this reason, the merit of the Bodhisattva is most honored and great, lofty and majestic; it is without beginning or end, boundless and limitless. This merit is difficult to extol and difficult to measure; these are the tenfold precepts of the Bodhisattva.

“The Bodhisattva constantly practices the four immeasurable minds (catvāry apramāṇāni), which are equal and without distinction. Having already believed in these merits, he attains the first stage (prathama-bhūmi); having attained the first stage, he attains the second; having attained the second, he attains the third; having attained the third, he attains the fourth; having attained the fourth, he attains the fifth; having attained the fifth, he attains the sixth; having attained the sixth, he attains the seventh; having attained the seventh, he attains the eighth; having attained the eighth, he attains the ninth; having attained the ninth, he attains the tenth; having attained the tenth stage, he becomes a Buddha and delivers all sentient beings. This is how the Bodhisattva accumulates merit and thereby brings himself to the attainment of the Way.”
If there are those who follow me in reciting this sutra, they shall eliminate all evils and swiftly attain Buddhahood.

Those who see it or hear it and rejoice at that moment shall eliminate the countless sins of their own bodies, cause them to attain the faith of the Ten Abodes, and thereby reach the realization of the Way.
One should always recite this sutra for one day and one night on the fifteenth day of the month; its merit surpasses that within the triple world.
Do not engage in conduct characterized by limitations, obstructions, or attachments, for such is a departure from merit and does not constitute the path of a bodhisattva.

The tenth recitation: "Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Dharma! Homage to the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus! Homage to all Bodhisattvas! Homage to the Bodhisattva Dānapāla! Homage to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī!"

The Bodhisattva always regards all people with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion; whether he sees the poor, the wealthy, the powerful, the noble, the lowly, the strong, the emaciated, or the timid, his mind constantly bears them in mind, desiring to bring them all to equality.

I constantly pray that the ten directions may be as level as water, without mountains or ravines; that people, whether rich or poor, shall be equal and without distinction; that their lifespans, whether long or short, shall be equal and without distinction; and that the noble and the lowly shall be equal and without distinction. May they share the same heart in seeking the Way, and may they always vow together to initiate the karma of the Mahāyāna. May all humans and non-humans alike resolve upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path; may they all possess wisdom and all practice giving, free from stinginess and greed; may they all uphold the sutras and precepts, be able to endure with patience, be capable of diligence, enter meditative concentration with a single mind, and see the transformative samādhis, all possessing *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means).
May those who are deluded quickly perceive the Right Path;
may those in darkness behold the light.
May all who are afflicted be healed and restored to health.
May those who are strong and healthy each manifest their physical vigor.
For those traveling by land, may humans, horses, carts, and oxen be robust; may the strength of human hands and feet be vigorous; and may their wealth and possessions be secure.

For those traveling by boat, whether going east, west, south, or north, or sailing up- or downstream, may they each obtain their wishes; may their ships and carriages be secure, and may their sails move with smooth efficiency.

In the marketplace, profits are a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or ten-thousandfold; he finds a secure place to dwell where buying and selling are convenient, and both the noble and the humble each obtain what they desire.
For those living at home, he ensures that wives, children, parents, and elders are all peaceful and secure, free from water and fire disasters, thieves and bandits, illness, and government officials.

Those who hold office shall always enjoy peace and security; they shall cherish and nurture the people with a compassionate heart, and their families shall be wealthy and prosperous, free from poverty, distress, or severe suffering.
This is the Bodhisattva’s practice of equality regarding the precepts during the eleven periods.
When good sons and good daughters hear this, they rejoice and all attain the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).

The celestial deities, earth deities, and mountain deities all come to attend and protect those who carry and uphold this sutra; no calamities whatsoever dare to offend them. This is what it means for a bodhisattva to have already attained supernormal powers.
The eleventh time: "Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Dharma! Homage to the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus! Homage to all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas! Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!"

The Bodhisattva attains the Way through the sequence of: first, counting; second, following; third, cessation; fourth, contemplation; fifth, returning; and sixth, purification. He attains the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, and Pratyekabuddha, yet he does not abide therein.

He attains the Buddha-way, manifesting the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, and a purple-golden complexion, as well as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, and the eight kinds of great sounds, yet he does not abide therein either.
The Bodhisattva gives rise to the enterprise of the Mahāyāna; by means of the *saṃnāhasaṃnaddha* (the armor of resolution), they deliver all humans and non-humans;
they manifest the *pāramitās* to all people; and through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, they rescue and protect all beings.
The Bodhisattva subdues those who are fierce and stubborn with gentleness and mildness; the Bodhisattva brings about harmony through *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means).
To all people, the Bodhisattva comforts them with humility, courtesy, kindness, and benevolence;
with harmony, joy, and gladness, the Bodhisattva subdues all evils and rebellions; with the power of the Path, the Bodhisattva delivers all from folly;
with purity, the Bodhisattva delivers all from craving and desire; and with great compassion, the Bodhisattva takes pity upon sentient beings. The Bodhisattva...
By practicing frugality, the bodhisattva renounces all wealth and treasures; by means of purity, the bodhisattva abandons all intoxication from wine;
by means of measured speech, the bodhisattva rectifies the mind and practices patience regarding the mouth; by means of walking meditation, the bodhisattva establishes himself in diligence;
by means of eating little, the bodhisattva eliminates sleep and lying down; by means of desirelessness, the bodhisattva makes the body light and robust.
The Bodhisattva nurtures the Way and its Virtue through freedom from anger; the Bodhisattva unites and gathers the multitude through freedom from jealousy;
the Bodhisattva causes their merit to flow back to all humans and non-humans.
These are the twelve-hour precepts of equal practice for a Bodhisattva, by which they rescue and deliver all sentient beings; such is the flying Bodhisattva.
Endowed with merit.
"Those who possess a virtuous mind and a good intention to hear this sutra, and who recite, chant, and read it, these are those in the tenth stage, the stage of non-regression (avaivartika)."

When a Bodhisattva enters water, he does not sink; when he enters fire, he is not burned. If one asks for his head, he gives his head; if one asks for his eyes, he gives his eyes; if one asks for his ears, he gives his ears; if one begs for his nose, he gives his nose. He casts himself into the mouth of a tiger, not begrudging his own body or life. These are the noble and sublime merits of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva—difficult to praise and difficult to measure, without end and without bottom, without limit and without bound, and beyond all calculation.

Each of you should respectfully uphold the World-Honored One’s sutras and precepts to protect your own conduct. Those whose actions accord with these sutras will find their every movement and posture appropriate; they should apply themselves with diligent effort, skillfully distance themselves from all evils, and never transgress them. Whoever transgresses them is not a bodhisattva.

This is what it means for a bodhisattva to be fully endowed with right precepts and to be in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*). Morning, evening, at dawn, and at dusk, they shall attain Buddhahood; the radiance of their marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) has already begun to manifest. This is the fulfillment of merit and the manifestation of all virtues; their majestic spiritual power is complete, and all pay them reverence, for none dare to oppose the bodhisattva.

When the Buddha had finished expounding the twelve periods of the perfect precepts for the merits of a bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, along with all the assembled bodhisattvas of supernatural powers, flying bodhisattvas, accomplished bodhisattvas, and manifested transformation bodhisattvas, as well as the bodhisattvas from the eight directions and the zenith and nadir—namely, Bhaṭṭika Bodhisattva, Rāṣṭrapāla Bodhisattva, Gopaka Bodhisattva, Nāgadatta Bodhisattva, Samudra Bodhisattva, Mahāsena Bodhisattva, Vaira Bodhisattva, Indradatta Bodhisattva, and Virūḍhaka Bodhisattva, totaling seventy-two thousand people—all leaped up with great joy and delight. Each manifested radiance that shone upon one another; they each rose, adjusted their robes, and prostrated themselves before the Buddha, touching their heads to the ground in homage.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the Bodhisattva Precepts during the twelfth period, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what merits does a bodhisattva attain these ten stages?"
“I only pray that the God among Gods will explain this in detail.
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent!”
Mañjuśrī! A bodhisattva mahāsattva brings much love and concern, and much peace and security. I shall now explain its essentials for you in full; listen attentively and receive it with careful heed.
Mañjuśrī replied, “I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha said:
“There are ten stages of bodhisattvas, each with its own distinctions of superiority and inferiority,
and they possess their own sequential order. Mañjuśrī asked, “What are these ten?”
“First is the Bodhisattva-dharma abiding in the *pāramitā* of patience (*kṣānti*). The Buddha said: “From the outset, one beholds the Teacher as peerlessly upright;

gazing upon his countenance, one never tires of it, and there is no one who can equal him. His nobility is unsurpassed, and his teachings cannot be excelled. Seeing the Buddha’s majestic power and ritual deportment thus, one gradually enters the path of the Buddha and is transformed by it. One guides others according to their inclinations, delivering them through instruction. Seeing those who undergo toil and suffering, one feels compassion for them all. Gradually understanding and comprehending the Buddha’s words, one places faith and turns toward them. One newly arouses the resolve to study the Buddha-way, desiring to fully comprehend it, and wishing to attain the Buddha’s wisdom regarding the ten difficult points.”
What are the ten difficult points?
They are the ten powers of a Buddha:
first, one should make offerings to the Buddha;... [and so forth].
Second, one should instruct others according to their inclinations;
third, one will be born into positions of honor and nobility in all places of rebirth;
fourth, there shall be none in the heavens above or the world below who can equal one.
Fifth, they shall fully attain the wisdom of the Buddha;
sixth, in every place where they are born throughout successive lifetimes, they shall behold countless Buddhas;
seventh, they shall fully attain all the Buddhist scriptures.
Eighth, they have completely transcended all birth and death;
ninth, they shall soon be liberated from this world;
tenth, they will fully deliver and liberate the people of the ten directions.
“What is the second dwelling, the dwelling of the Bodhisattva’s *asaṃbhava* (non-arising) Dharma?
The Buddha said:
“There are ten intentions with which one contemplates the people of the ten directions.”
What are the ten mental states?
First, to fully contemplate the goodness of the world;
second, to purify the mind.
Third, all are at peace;
fourth, the mind is gentle and supple;
fifth, there is universal and impartial love.
Sixth, one’s mind should intend only to give in charity to others;
seventh, one’s mind should protect all beings;
eighth, one should contemplate that others and one’s own body are no different.
Ninth, one should mentally regard the people of the ten directions as one's own teachers;
tenth, one should mentally regard the people of the ten directions as Buddhas.
An Ajāśvita Bodhisattva’s dharma requires that they study many sutras extensively.
Having studied many scriptures, one should dwell alone in the mountains;
dwelling alone in the mountains, one should attend upon a virtuous teacher;
attending upon a virtuous teacher, one should remain by the side of that teacher, be easy to direct, be timely, and act with courage according to the occasion.
Once one’s actions are courageous, one should train in entering wisdom; the teachings received within the mind should be fully retained;
having fully retained them, those retained teachings should not be forgotten;
and once they are not forgotten, one should dwell peacefully in the mountains.
Why is this? Because it benefits the people of the ten directions.
What is the analogy for the third stage, the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-abiding?
The Buddha said:
"One enters into all dharmas by means of ten matters.
What are these ten matters?"
First, all that exists is impermanent;
second, all that exists is subject to suffering;
third, all that exists is empty.
Fourth, all that exists is not mine; fifth, all that exists has no owner;
sixth, all that exists is without benefit.
Seventh, all that exists has no place of rest;
eighth, all that exists has no place of abiding;
ninth, all that exists has no place of attachment.
Tenth, all dharmas, being entirely non-existent, are fully contained within a single dharma, and that single dharma is fully contained within all dharmas.
This is the teaching of the Bodhisattva Asaṃga.

"What are the four abodes? What is the bodhisattva-dharma-abode of Yāmaki? The Buddha said: "There are ten matters by which one constantly aspires to be born in the presence of a Buddha: 1. One constantly aspires to be born in the presence of a Buddha. 2. One constantly aspires to see the Buddha’s body. 3. One constantly aspires to hear the Dharma from the Buddha. 4. One constantly aspires to serve the Buddha with all manner of offerings. 5. One constantly aspires to be born in the same assembly as the Buddha. 6. One constantly aspires to receive the Buddha’s prediction of future enlightenment. 7. One constantly aspires to be born in the Buddha-lands where the Buddhas dwell. 8. One constantly aspires to attain the Buddha’s supernormal powers. 9. One constantly aspires to be born in the presence of the Buddhas who have attained parinirvāṇa. 10. One constantly aspires to attain the Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom."
First, not returning;
second, reflecting deeply on the Buddha;
third, reflecting deeply on the Dharma.
Fourth, to keep the Sangha of bhikṣus in mind while beholding the people of the ten directions;
fifth, to contemplate that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic existence;
sixth, that the buddha-fields of the ten directions are all empty space.
Seventh, that which was accomplished through past lives is utterly non-existent;
eighth, all that exists is like an illusion and entirely empty;
ninth, all diligent efforts and hardships are non-existent.
Tenth, nirvāṇa and space are likewise non-existent; for this reason, one is born into the Buddha-dharma.
This is the teaching of the Bodhisattva Yamamati.

"What are the five abodes that constitute the Bodhisattva-dharma-abode of the 'Wave Simile' (taraṅga-upama)? The Buddha said: "There are ten matters by which all merits performed deliver beings throughout the ten directions: 1. To cause all sentient beings to attain the fruit of the Stream-enterer (srotāpanna); 2. To cause all sentient beings to attain the fruit of the Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin); 3. To cause all sentient beings to attain the fruit of the Non-returner (anāgāmin); 4. To cause all sentient beings to attain the fruit of Arhatship; 5. To cause all sentient beings to attain the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood; 6. To cause all sentient beings to attain the stage of the Bodhisattva who has entered the path of certain assurance (niyāmāvakrānti); 7. To cause all sentient beings to attain the stage of the Bodhisattva who has reached the ultimate limit; 8. To cause all sentient beings to attain the stage of the Bodhisattva who has attained the power of non-retrogression; 9. To cause all sentient beings to attain the stage of the Bodhisattva who has reached the final birth; 10. To cause all sentient beings to attain the stage of the Tathāgata."
First, to protect all people of the ten directions;
second, to mindfully contemplate the virtues of all people of the ten directions;
third, to mindfully contemplate all people of the ten directions so as to cause them all to dwell in peace and security.
Fourth, to love all people of the ten directions;
fifth, to compassionately care for all people of the ten directions;
sixth, to keep all people of the ten directions in mind so as not to allow them to commit evil.
Seventh, to lead all people of the ten directions into the bodhisattva path;
eighth, to completely purify all people of the ten directions;
ninth, to fully deliver and liberate all people of the ten directions.
Tenth, to cause all people throughout the ten directions to enter parinirvāṇa.
These are the three types of parinirvāṇa in the bodhisattva’s teaching of the *pāyus*.
What are the three types of abiding in the dharma for the bodhisattva at the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī-bhūmi*)?
The Buddha said:
"There are ten dharmas of profound compassion and loving-kindness:
first, when others speak of the Buddha’s virtues or faults, one’s mind remains without change."
Second, when preaching the Dharma of the sutras, there is no difference between their wholesome and unwholesome minds;
third, when preaching concerning bodhisattvas, there is no difference between their wholesome and unwholesome minds;
fourth, when seeking those on the path of a bodhisattva, they share with one another no difference between their wholesome and unwholesome minds.
Fifth, people say that the minds of those in the ten directions, whether many or few, are no different;
sixth, observing the people of the ten directions as they speak of one another’s good and evil deeds, their minds are no different;
seventh, among them there are those who say that the minds of the people of the ten directions, whether easy to liberate or difficult to liberate, are no different.
Eighth, if someone says that whether the Dharma is taught extensively or briefly, the mind remains without difference;
ninth, if someone says that whether the Dharma is taught as being subject to destruction or not, the mind remains without difference;
tenth, whether there is a locus of dharmas or no locus of dharmas, the mind remains without difference.
These are the three kinds of teachings for the Bodhisattvas who have attained the stage of *A* (Non-retrogression).
"What is the dwelling of the *Avaivartika* (Non-retrogressive) Bodhisattva in the seventh stage?
The Buddha said:
“There are ten matters in which one remains firm and unshakable:
first, one does not waver or turn back regardless of whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha;
second, one does not waver or turn back regardless of whether there is the Dharma or no Dharma;”
Third, there is the non-retrogression of one who possesses the bodhisattva-nature and one who does not;
fourth, there is the non-retrogression of one who seeks the bodhisattva path and one who does not seek it;
fifth, there is the attainment of non-retrogression through upholding the Dharma.
Sixth, whether there have been past Buddhas or there have been no past Buddhas, one does not waver or turn back;
seventh, whether there will be future Buddhas or there will be no future Buddhas, one does not waver or turn back;
eighth, whether there is a present Buddha or there is no present Buddha, one does not waver or turn back.
Ninth, the Buddha’s wisdom is neither exhausted nor inexhaustible, and it does not waver or regress;
tenth, regarding the affairs of future, past, and present times, however many varieties there may be, he does not waver or regress.
This is the teaching for the *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
"What is the eighth dwelling, the *kumārabhūta*—the bodhisattva stage of the youthful male?
The Buddha said:
“A Bodhisattva dwells in ten matters:
first, his bodily conduct, verbal speech, and mental thoughts are all pure;
second, no one is able to find fault with him.”
Third, with a single turn of thought, he knows the place where he intends to be reborn;
fourth, he knows who among the people of the ten directions possesses a compassionate heart;
fifth, he fully knows all that is trusted and relied upon by the people of the ten directions.
Sixth, he fully knows the various kinds of people throughout the ten directions;
seventh, he fully knows the actions performed by the people throughout the ten directions;
eighth, he fully knows the formation and destruction of all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions.
Ninth, they attain the power of the divine feet (ṛddhipāda) and can fly to wherever they wish to go;
tenth, all things are completely pure and clean.
These constitute the teaching for the Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva.
“What is the metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-abiding in the ninth stage?
The Buddha said:
“It is attained through ten matters:”
First, he fully knows all those born throughout the ten directions;
second, he fully knows all the bonds of affection held by those throughout the ten directions;
third, he fully knows the origins and ends of what those throughout the ten directions contemplate, as well as where they have come from.
Fourth, they fully know the past lives and the destinies of all people throughout the ten directions;
fifth, they fully know the various kinds of dharmas;
sixth, they fully know the various kinds of transformations conceived by all people throughout the ten directions.
Seventh, they fully know the excellence, evil, and destruction of all Buddha-fields;
eighth, they fully know the infinite matters of the past, future, and present;
ninth, they fully know the equality and inequality of people throughout the ten directions.
Tenth, he teaches people throughout the ten directions and fully understands the preaching of the Dharma of space.
This is the teaching method of the Bodhisattva Upāli.
"What is the Dharma-abiding of the Bodhisattva Akṣobhya among the Ten Abidings?
The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva enters into the ten knowledges, they are able to discern and understand ten matters:
first, by what cause should one cause the various buddha-fields of the ten directions to tremble?"
Second, I shall clearly illuminate countless Buddha-fields;
third, I shall daily appoint Bodhisattvas within countless Buddha-fields;
fourth, I shall daily deliver and liberate the people within countless Buddha-fields.
Fifth, I shall bring peace and security to the sentient beings within countless Buddha-fields;
sixth, there shall be no one throughout the ten directions who does not hear my voice and attain joyful liberation;
seventh, I shall mindfully cause all the people of the ten directions to attain the Buddha-way, so that they all renounce their homes to become śramaṇas.
Eighth, I fully know the thoughts of good and evil entertained by people throughout the ten directions;
ninth, I shall cause all people throughout the ten directions to be inwardly established within the Buddha-way and cause them all to resolve upon the mind of a bodhisattva;
tenth, I shall bring all people throughout the ten directions to liberation.

This Bodhisattva Ayurāja was utterly unable to comprehend the conduct of the body, the speech uttered by the mouth, the thoughts conceived by the mind, or the deeds performed by the A-vyaya (A-yü-yen) Bodhisattva; he was utterly unable to comprehend the affairs of the A-vyaya Bodhisattva, nor could he know his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), nor his flight, nor could he ever fathom the past, future, or present affairs of the A-vyaya Bodhisattva.
"This is the teaching for the Bodhisattva of the Unexcelled Rank (A-vy-yan).
Thus spoke the Buddha in the *Bodhisattva-adhyātma-śīla-sūtra*.
